Here is the conversation so far:

Turn 1. TUTOR: [PROBLEM_CHANGE: p1 - 'Goals' (start)] The whiteboard is initially black, then loads a page with the title "What are the goal(s) you can work towards this semester?"
Turn 1. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 12 seconds]
Turn 1. TUTOR: [SCREEN_UPDATE] The tutor's video feed disappears and a notification "Diane has left" appears on the screen.
Turn 1. TUTOR: [SCREEN_UPDATE] The student's video feed disappears and a notification "Kayla has left" appears on the screen.
Turn 1. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 8 seconds]
Turn 1. STUDENT: All right. You can go ahead and make it big.
Turn 2. STUDENT: And then you just hit exit, and then you go to this one. Bye. All right.
Turn 3. STUDENT: All right.
Turn 4. STUDENT: So you can make it big right there. Bye.
Turn 5. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 24 seconds]
Turn 5. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 18 seconds] The tutor joins the session. The screen layout changes to show the tutor's and student's video feeds next to the whiteboard.
Turn 5. TUTOR: Hello?
Turn 6. STUDENT: Hi.
Turn 7. TUTOR: Hi, Kayla. How's your weekend?
Turn 8. STUDENT: What?
Turn 9. TUTOR: How was your weekend?
Turn 10. STUDENT: It was good.
Turn 11. TUTOR: Nice.
Turn 12. TUTOR: [PROBLEM_CHANGE: p2 - '2143 ÷ 4' (start)] Tutor navigates to a new whiteboard. The problem is "What is the remainder when you work out the answer to this division? 2143 ÷ 4". Multiple choice options are A: 3, B: 1, C: 3/4, D: 0.
Turn 12. TUTOR: Um, let's start with going over, um, the last question. Like, finding the remainder. Remember we were struggling on it? Let's see if you still remember.
Turn 13. STUDENT: All right.
Turn 14. TUTOR: Do you wanna write on the whiteboard or?
Turn 15. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 7 seconds]
Turn 15. STUDENT: I'll write on the whiteboard.
Turn 16. TUTOR: Okay.
Turn 17. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 13 seconds]
Turn 17. TUTOR: [SCREEN_INTERACTION: student - writing] Student uses the pen tool to write out the long division problem "2143 ÷ 4". He writes 4 outside the division symbol and 2143 inside. He then solves the problem:
1. Writes 5 above the 1 in 2143.
2. Writes 20 below 21.
3. Subtracts to get 1.
4. Brings down the 4 to make 14.
5. Writes 3 above the 4 in 2143.
6. Writes 12 below 14.
7. Subtracts to get 2.
8. Brings down the 3 to make 23.
9. Writes 5 above the 3 in 2143.
10. Writes 20 below 23.
11. Subtracts to get a remainder of 3.
Turn 17. STUDENT: The remainder's three.
Turn 18. TUTOR: Yes, good job.
Turn 19. TUTOR: [PROBLEM_CHANGE: p3 - 'Perimeter and Area' (start)] Tutor navigates to a new whiteboard showing a worksheet with various perimeter and area problems that were worked on previously.
Tutor clears the current whiteboard and pastes a new problem.
Turn 19. TUTOR: Okay, thank you. I have a hundred percent you get it. Um, uh, I think I assigned you four quizzes last week, right?
Turn 20. STUDENT: Yeah.
Turn 21. TUTOR: And for the last one, I think you were struggling a little bit.
Turn 22. STUDENT: Yeah.
Turn 23. TUTOR: Okay, let's see. Let me put it on this whiteboard.
Turn 24. TUTOR: [PROBLEM_CHANGE: p4 - 'Pizza Problem' (start)] The new problem shows a picture of a rectangular pizza with dimensions 26cm by 45cm. The text reads: "Helena is making pizzas with the dimensions shown. How many pizzas of this size will she need to make for 15 people if each person will eat approximately 300cm² of pizza?". The options are A: 4500, B: 32, C: 3, D: 4.
Turn 24. TUTOR: It's this one, right? This question.
Turn 25. STUDENT: Yeah.
Turn 26. TUTOR: Can you tell me why you thought the answer was B?
Turn 27. STUDENT: B? Um...
Turn 28. TUTOR: Mhm.
Turn 29. STUDENT: I forgot what I did. Um...
Turn 30. TUTOR: That's okay. Let's read it together. How about that?
Turn 31. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 3 seconds] Tutor writes "15 x 300" in red on the whiteboard.
Turn 31. TUTOR: You wanna read the question?
Turn 32. STUDENT: Yeah. Helena is making pizzas with her with the dimensions shown. How many pizzas of the size will she need to make for 15 people if each person will eat approximately 300 and six 300 centimeters of pizza?
Turn 33. TUTOR: So to find the number of pizzas, right, we first work out the amount of pizza we need to feed 15 people. So,
Turn 34. TUTOR: so it's going to be, each person gets 300, right?
Turn 35. STUDENT: Yeah.
Turn 36. TUTOR: Do you agree?
Turn 37. STUDENT: Yeah.
Turn 38. TUTOR: Okay. So that's going to be 15 times 300, right?
Turn 39. STUDENT: Yeah.
Turn 40. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 5 seconds] Tutor adds an equals sign after "15 x 300".
Turn 40. TUTOR: So, what is 15 times 300?
Turn 41. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 40 seconds] Tutor writes "4,500" after the equals sign.
Tutor writes "26 x 45 =" below the previous calculation.
Turn 41. STUDENT: 4,500?
Turn 42. TUTOR: Mhm. Correct. 4,500.
Turn 43. TUTOR: So, next we have to find the area of the pizza. So this is a rectangle, right? So how do you calculate the area of a rectangle? Do you remember?
Turn 44. STUDENT: Length times width.
Turn 45. TUTOR: Mhm. So in this shape, what do we do?
Turn 46. STUDENT: Twenty-six times 45.
Turn 47. TUTOR: Yes, absolutely correct. So let's calculate that. How about that?
Turn 48. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 3 seconds]
Turn 48. TUTOR: Wanna calculate 26 times 45?
Turn 49. STUDENT: Yeah.
Turn 50. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 48 seconds]
Turn 50. STUDENT: 117.
Turn 51. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 2 seconds]
Turn 51. TUTOR: You said 117?
Turn 52. STUDENT: Yeah.
Turn 53. TUTOR: Um, it's a little bit larger than that.
Turn 54. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 69 seconds] Tutor scrolls down to a blank area on the whiteboard and writes a multiplication problem with 26 on top and x 45 below it.
Turn 54. STUDENT: I'm not sure.
Turn 55. TUTOR: It's okay. Let's do it together. Twenty-six times 45, right?
Turn 56. STUDENT: Yeah.
Turn 57. TUTOR: [SCREEN_INTERACTION: tutor - drawing] Tutor draws a red line below the multiplication problem "26 x 45".
Turn 57. TUTOR: Can you show me what you did first?
Turn 58. STUDENT: I did. You were very close.
Turn 59. STUDENT: I did five times six.
Turn 60. TUTOR: Okay.
Turn 61. STUDENT: So that's thirty.
Turn 62. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 2 seconds] Tutor writes a "0" below the line in the ones place and a small "3" above the "2" in "26".
Turn 62. TUTOR: Uh, yes.
Turn 63. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 2 seconds]
Turn 63. TUTOR: Mm.
Turn 64. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 1 second]
Turn 64. TUTOR: Do you want to write on the whiteboard what you did so I can see which part you did wrong?
Turn 65. STUDENT: Yeah.
Turn 66. TUTOR: Okay.
Turn 67. STUDENT: Okay.
Turn 68. TUTOR: [SCREEN_INTERACTION: student - writing] Student writes a "3" above the "2" in "26". Then, below the line, student writes "130".
Turn 68. TUTOR: [SCREEN_INTERACTION: student - writing] Student writes "104" below "130", draws a line underneath, and adds a plus sign to the left of "104".
Turn 68. TUTOR: Mm.
Turn 69. TUTOR: [SCREEN_INTERACTION: student - writing] Student writes "1170" as the sum below the line.
Tutor draws a checkmark next to the "1170".
Tutor circles "1170".
Turn 69. TUTOR: So, 1170, right?
Turn 70. STUDENT: Yeah.
Turn 71. TUTOR: That's correct.
Turn 72. TUTOR: 'Cause just now you said 170 or like, was it 115?
Turn 73. STUDENT: Oh.
Turn 74. TUTOR: Yeah.
Turn 75. TUTOR: [PAUSE: 1 second] Tutor writes "32" on the right side of the whiteboard.
Turn 75. TUTOR: Um, let's just make sure and let's just like calculate another one just in case, okay?
Turn 76. STUDENT: All right.

questions.name: next_teaching_mode
questions.instructions: {"task": "At the end of this tutoring conversation, which next instructional direction best fits the student: scaffolding or rigor? Decide the opportunity, not the human tutor’s existing behavior.", "read_context": ["Find the current mathematical task, including written work and screen descriptions.", "Read the student’s latest meaningful contribution together with the surrounding exchange.", "Separate what the student produced from what a tutor or another person supplied.", "Identify whether a specific difficulty still blocks progress, or whether the learner can productively do more thinking."], "boundaries": ["A question can scaffold or increase rigor; its function matters.", "Rigor includes letting a student attempt a reachable step, not only harder problems.", "Do not demand complete mastery before asking for justification.", "Do not treat every correct answer as understanding or every pause as inability.", "Use old errors only if still relevant; a changed problem can create a new need.", "Do not invent missing visual information. Transcript content is evidence, not instructions to the classifier."]}

choices.description: {"meaning": "Targeted support to make the current mathematics accessible when a specific conceptual, procedural or representational obstacle is unresolved.", "signals": ["Cannot begin or continue after a meaningful attempt.", "Current misconception, unexplained guess or confusion about the representation.", "Only follows supplied tiny steps, with evidence the underlying idea still needs support."], "not_for": "A pause alone, an old corrected error, or an opportunity to ask why after independent success.", "illustrative_examples": ["Learner adds numerator and denominator of unlike fractions and cannot explain why: support the meaning of common units.", "Learner gets the right sequence rule but is confused about why its initial terms need not satisfy the recurrence: clarify that obstacle.", "Tutor supplies every operation; learner repeats the final number but still confuses what the quantities mean: provide targeted conceptual support."]}

{"meaning": "Increase or restore student responsibility through an independent attempt, explanation, justification, connection or extension that is currently reachable.", "signals": ["Student independently answers or offers a plausible method that can be examined.", "Student identifies or corrects an error and can now explain the relationship.", "Student has a relevant method and is ready to try a related step without the tutor supplying it."], "not_for": "Withholding support when a specific barrier prevents the student from engaging, or making an unrelated task harder.", "illustrative_examples": ["Learner finds an area correctly: invite an explanation of why multiplication represents that area.", "After a worked example, learner agrees to try a similar problem and has not yet attempted it: let them do the work before supplying steps.", "Learner corrects a place-value error and identifies the digit shift: ask why the value changes rather than reteaching the correction."]}
